quote: {'authors': [{'family': 'Sall', 'given': 'J'}, {'family': 'Brenner', 'given': 'L'}, {'family': 'Millikan', 'given': 'Bell AM'}, {'family': 'Colston', 'given': 'MJ'}], 'doi': '10.7326/M19-0687', 'journal': 'Ann Intern Med', 'organization': '', 'pages': '343-353', 'pmid': '31450237', 'title': 'Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide: Synopsis of the 2019 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and U.S. Department of Defense Clinical Practice Guidelines', 'url': 'https://doi.org/10.7326/M19-0687', 'volume': '171', 'year': 2019}
problem: The source is registered as type 'guideline', but it is the synopsis of the 2019 VA/DoD suicide-risk CPG. The 2024 CPG replaced that guideline, and the registry already lists the 2024 CPG as va-dod-suicide-cpg-2024. The 2024 update has its own Annals synopsis. The author list also has a parsing error: the author is Millikan Bell AM, but it is split as family 'Millikan', given 'Bell AM'.
whyItMatters: Any page that cites sall-2019 as guidance teaches the 2019 recommendation set, which had 22 recommendations. The 2024 update has 24 recommendations built on a 2018–2023 evidence review, adds a CBT recommendation for people with prior self-directed violence, and gives clozapine and ketamine a role in managing suicide risk. Two different VA/DoD 'current' guidelines in one registry is also a citation inconsistency.
evidence: PubMed 39903866: Brenner LA et al. 'Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide: Synopsis of the 2024 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and U.S. Department of Defense Clinical Practice Guidelines.' Ann Intern Med 2025;178(3):416-425, doi:10.7326/ANNALS-24-01938. Its abstract says the 2024 CPG 'updated the 2019 joint clinical practice guideline'. PubMed 31450237 confirms the 2019 synopsis identity and the author 'Millikan Bell, Amy M'.

quote: but against active controls MBT(-A) did not prove more efficacious except for adult borderline personality disorder symptoms at g = -0.56
problem: The span names the comparators as 'control interventions (TAU, SCM)'. Treatment as usual is not an active control. The claim therefore makes the null result sound weaker than it is: MBT(-A) also failed to beat TAU for self-harm.
whyItMatters: A learner would conclude that MBT only fails to beat other structured therapies and so still beats usual care for self-harm. The paper does not support that, and the page could be used to favour MBT referral over other options for self-harm.
evidence: Hajek Gross C et al., Suicide Life Threat Behav 2024;54(2):317-337 (PMID 38279664, doi:10.1111/sltb.13044). The abstract says: 'when compared to control interventions (TAU, SCM), MBT(-A) did not prove to be more efficacious'.
correction: but against control interventions (treatment as usual or structured clinical management) MBT(-A) did not prove more efficacious except for adult borderline personality disorder symptoms at g = -0.56

quote: > Lethal means assessment reduced the risk of a suicide attempt or death within 180 days from 3.3 to 0.83%.
problem: The claim stands alone as a causal fact: roughly a 75% relative reduction. It leaves out that this is a quasi-experimental observational analysis (an instrumental-variable design on EHR data) in patients who endorsed suicidal ideation on the PHQ-9. The authors themselves warn that unmeasured co-occurring prevention practices may contribute to the effect.
whyItMatters: Learners and residents may quote 'asking about means cuts suicide attempts by three-quarters' as a trial result. That overstates certainty in exactly the lethal-means teaching this surface (exp_family) supports. The direction of the finding is right, but the size and the causal wording are not licensed.
evidence: Boggs JM et al., J Gen Intern Med 2020;35(6):1709-1714 (PMID 32040838). The title reads 'A Quasi-Experimental Analysis…'. Setting: Kaiser Permanente Colorado adults with suicidal ideation on the PHQ-9, 2010–2016. Limitations: 'Unmeasured suicide prevention practices that co-occur with lethal means assessment may contribute to the effects observed.'
correction: > In a quasi-experimental analysis of patients with suicide ideation reported on the PHQ-9, lethal means assessment reduced the risk of a suicide attempt or death within 180 days from 3.3 to 0.83% — an observational estimate, not a randomized trial result.
verified: PubMed abstract, PMID 32040838. Optionally extend the stored span to include the authors' limitations sentence.

quote: while severity of depression and suicidal ideation decreased comparably in both groups and outcomes were comparable between the two groups at 12-month follow-up.
problem: The claim, typed 'mixed', leaves out the one outcome in the span that favoured the comparator: 'After 6 months of treatment, the rate of major depressive disorder was significantly lower in the SSRI/M arm compared with the DBT arm.' Two-thirds of the sample had comorbid MDD.
whyItMatters: A resident reading the claim alone would think DBT matched or beat SSRI management on every outcome. They might then treat an SSRI as dispensable in a patient with BPD and comorbid major depression, when the trial showed a lower MDD rate on the SSRI.
evidence: Brodsky BS et al., Am J Psychiatry 2025;182(12):1083-1092 (PMID 41190740). The stored span contains the MDD sentence verbatim. The PubMed abstract adds that survival analysis showed no difference in the risk of a suicide attempt.
correction: while severity of depression and suicidal ideation decreased comparably in both groups, the rate of major depressive disorder after 6 months was significantly lower in the SSRI/M arm, and outcomes were comparable between the two groups at 12-month follow-up.

quote: In a cohort comparison of 1640 emergency-department patients
problem: The claim drops the population and setting given in the span: suicidal patients in Veterans Health Administration EDs, with non-randomized intervention and control sites.
whyItMatters: The 45%/OR 0.56 figure gets generalized to all ED populations. Learners should know it comes from a VHA cohort comparison, not an RCT in a general civilian population.
evidence: Stanley B, Brown GK et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(9):894-900 (PMID 29998307). The span says: '9 EDs (5 intervention sites and 4 control sites) in Veterans Health Administration hospital EDs'.
correction: In a cohort comparison of 1640 suicidal patients treated in Veterans Health Administration emergency departments
verified: span text (verbatim in chunk); recall of the paper

quote: Across 53 studies, benzodiazepine treatment of catatonia produced an overall response rate of 77%
problem: The span says most of the 53 studies were case series using lorazepam, which are uncontrolled. 'Produced' states an uncontrolled pooled response rate as a causal efficacy figure, and the claim leaves out the design.
whyItMatters: The 77% is quoted as if it were a trial response rate. The number is right, but learners should know it rests on case series and has no controlled comparator. The authors call for controlled studies.
evidence: Bot L et al., Acta Psychiatr Scand 2026;154(2):99-115 (PMID 42009596). The abstract says: 'Most were case series using lorazepam'; 'the need for… well-designed controlled studies'.
correction: Across 53 studies, mostly case series using lorazepam, benzodiazepine treatment of catatonia was associated with an overall response rate of 77%

quote: to 27 participants produced reductions in depressive symptoms at day 7
problem: This is an uncontrolled, single-arm quality-improvement pilot (n = 27). 'Produced' makes a causal claim that the design cannot support, even though the claim goes on to say 'pilot evidence'.
whyItMatters: Learners may count day-7 symptom change as an effect of caring contacts. With no comparator, it could just as well be the natural course after discharge.
evidence: Steinberg R et al., Suicide Life Threat Behav 2024;54(6):1041-1052 (PMID 38934489), described as a 'three-phase, mixed-method quality-improvement study'. Phase 3 was an uncontrolled pilot. The span says 'participants demonstrated reductions'.
correction: to 27 participants were followed by reductions in depressive symptoms at day 7

quote: paracetamol pack size limitation reduced self-poisoning admissions, and bans on highly hazardous pesticides reduced suicide rates.
problem: The span qualifies the paracetamol finding with 'with mixed impacts on mortality', and the barrier finding with 'although primary study overlap was high'. The claim drops both hedges.
whyItMatters: A learner could cite pack-size limits as a proven way to reduce suicide deaths. The overview found only a clear drop in admissions, with mixed results on mortality.
evidence: Steeg S et al., BMJ Ment Health 2025;28(1) (PMID 41365522). The abstract says: 'Paracetamol pack size limitation reduced self-poisoning admissions, with mixed impacts on mortality'; 12/20 reviews were rated critically low quality.
correction: paracetamol pack size limitation reduced self-poisoning admissions with mixed impacts on mortality, and bans on highly hazardous pesticides reduced suicide rates.

quote: > Across 53 randomised controlled trials, family intervention may decrease the frequency of relapse (RR 0.55, NNT 7) and may also reduce hospital admission (RR 0.78).
problem: The claim credits both estimates to all 53 RCTs. The span gives relapse from 32 RCTs (n = 2981) and admission from 8 RCTs (n = 481; CI 0.6 to 1.0, touching no effect). It also drops the span's caveat that small negative studies may have been missed. This is the same error class as prior finding A4-F001 (cohen-chazani).
whyItMatters: It inflates the apparent evidence base of the admission estimate, which comes from 481 patients with a confidence interval reaching 1.0, and hides the possible publication bias.
evidence: Pharoah F et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2010, CD000088.pub3 (PMID 21154340). The stored span says: 'n = 2981, 32 RCTs, RR 0.55… n = 481, 8 RCTs, RR 0.78 CI 0.6 to 1.0'.
correction: > In a review of 53 randomised controlled trials, family intervention may decrease the frequency of relapse (32 RCTs, n = 2981; RR 0.55, NNT 7), although some small but negative studies might not have been identified, and may also reduce hospital admission (8 RCTs, n = 481; RR 0.78, CI 0.6 to 1.0).

quote: while the difference between activity scheduling and cognitive therapy was 0.02 and non-significant at follow-up — activation is a treatment in its own right, not a preliminary to cognitive work.
problem: The claim merges two timepoints: 0.02 is the post-test difference, and non-significance at follow-up is a separate result. It also adds an interpretive conclusion ('a treatment in its own right, not a preliminary to cognitive work') that the span does not license. That breaks the registry's own rule that every claim be licensed by the stored span.
whyItMatters: The comparison rests on 10 small studies from a 2007 meta-analysis. Stating the gloss as the paper's finding overstates it. The practical point (activation alone works about as well as cognitive therapy) holds without the gloss.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., Clin Psychol Rev 2007;27:318-326 (PMID 17184887). The span says: 'In ten studies… the pooled effect size… was 0.02. The differences… at follow-up were also non-significant.'
correction: while in ten studies the difference between activity scheduling and cognitive therapy was 0.02 at post-test and also non-significant at follow-up — activity scheduling performed as well as cognitive therapy.

quote: Flexibly interweaving risk assessment into therapeutic conversation was beneficial to the alliance with suicidal clients and enhanced their safety — weaving risk assessment into the conversation rather than bolting it on.
problem: The source is a qualitative meta-ethnography of client and therapist perspectives (37 papers). The claim, typed 'positive', states 'enhanced their safety' as an outcome without saying these are perceived benefits from qualitative synthesis, not measured safety outcomes.
whyItMatters: On suicide-risk teaching surfaces, residents may cite this as evidence that conversational risk assessment reduces suicidal behaviour. The source measured no such outcome.
evidence: Huggett C et al., Clin Psychol Rev 2024;113:102469 (PMID 39098267): 'A systematic review and meta-ethnography of client and therapist perspectives…'. The span begins 'Thirty-seven papers were included, generating two overarching themes'.
correction: Flexibly interweaving risk assessment into therapeutic conversation was beneficial to the alliance with suicidal clients and enhanced their safety — as reported by clients and therapists across 37 qualitative papers, not a measured outcome; weave risk assessment into the conversation rather than bolting it on.
